newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Ansett shopping for eight new planes.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Ansett shopping for eight new planes.

text.p: Loss-making airline Ansett Australia is shopping for eight new aircraft in an effort to turn the company around and prepare it for listing, Ansett executive chairman Rod Eddington said on Wednesday.
Eddington, in his first major speech since he was appointed to run Ansett, said the new aircraft were crucial to simplify the airline's complex, inefficient fleet structure.
"Unless Ansett changes, it won't survive in the medium to long term," he told the National Aviation Press Club.
Ansett also needs to sell out of non-core businesses such as resorts and forge alliances around the globe, he said, naming Singapore Airlines and United Airlines as potential partners.
"We are talking to Singapore Airlines, but we are talking to a lot of other people as well," said the former Cathay Pacific Airways managing director.
Ansett is owned half by Air New Zealand, its "bedrock" alliance partner, and media group News Corp.
Ansett International, the airline's fledgling regional carrier flying to seven Asian destinations, is owned 49 percent by Ansett and 51 percent by Australian institutions.
Ansett runs seven different aircraft types but aims to pare this back to five to improve efficiency.
On some days, Ansett now runs four different aircraft on routes that can be serviced with one or two, Eddington said.
"We have got to simplify the business," he added.
The contract for the new aircraft, said by commentators to be worth over A$2 billion, is a close contest between European aircraft consortium Airbus Industrie and U.S.-based Boeing Co..
It is a close call between Airbus's A330-200 and Boeing's 767-300, Eddington said, adding: "It's the closest one I have been part of."
Eddington suggested two to three years were needed to get Ansett in shape for a possible float on the Australian share market.
"There's no point in taking any business to the market until it's in pretty robust shape. Ansett is a long, long way away from that now," he said.
